deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no derivation, formula or computation. It is a page of philosophical reading notes in Latin and German, copied excerpts with a few references. It continues the excerpt begun on the previous page from J. F. Herbart's 'Theoriae de attractione elementorum principia metaphysica' (Königsberg 1812), §27, and the reading of Herbart's Werke, Bd. VII, 'Über Kategorien und Conjunctionen', which continues on the next page.

(1) Top paragraph, Latin, Herbart §27 Scholion, end. Herbart says Leibniz preferred to rest in a 'heap of faults' (the vinculum substantiale) rather than re-examine the notion of the continuum. He calls that notion 'no less hostile to metaphysics than necessary to geometry', but claims it can be purged so as to satisfy both. Herbart announces two later results:
- From the attraction theory itself it will follow that neither the continuum nor the contiguum (§18) is to be used per se to explain how matter fills space.
- Instead the matter reduces to 'imaginary notions' (notiones imaginariae, §§21-22). These may be applied to matter without error, provided one first establishes that the simple beings (simplicia, Herbart's 'Realen') are not affected by them.
The reason given is that no spatially derived notions at all apply to simples, by the thesis of this §. In that respect imaginary and consistent notions do not differ.

(2) Leibniz excerpts, from Opera ed. Dutens, Tom. II, pp. 320-322, the Des Bosses correspondence on the vinculum substantiale:
- p. 322: corporeal (composite) substance is restricted to living beings, i.e. organic machines of nature. Everything else is a mere aggregate ('substantiata'), which is one only per accidens.
- p. 321: the entelechy of a composite substance always accompanies its dominant monad. Monad plus entelechy gives the substantial form of the animal.
- p. 320: relations joining two monads are in neither monad but only in the mind, unless one adds a real or substantial bond that is the subject of the common predicates. There is no accident with 'one foot in one subject and the other in another'.
These quotations document Herbart's critique of the vinculum.

(3) References:
- ἄποιος ὕλη (quality-less matter). Cf. Herbart, Einleitung in die Philosophie, 3rd ed., §166, on Anaximander's ἄπειρον.
- Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism (Πυρρώνειοι ὑποτυπώσεις) III, 4.
- 'quantum extensionis und Distanz': cf. Metaphysik §116, Psychologie Bd. 2 §144, Werke VI 311, Werke III 417, Bd. I §141.

(4) German excerpts, Herbart Werke VII, 'Über Kategorien und Conjunctionen' §§63, 69, 70, pp. 556-560.
- ποσόν (quantity) and ποιόν (quality) are treated as sub-kinds of 'Eigenschaft' (property).
- Aristotle lists ποσόν and ποιόν side by side, with πρός τι (relation) in between, yet quality-concepts turn up unexpectedly. 'More or less' is a recurring question for each category.
- §70: the distinction of continuous and discrete magnitude matters because for Aristotle μᾶλλον καὶ ἧττον (more and less, i.e. intensive degree) has a different origin from ποσόν. Intensive magnitude lets one follow infinitely small increments in thought, or fix a point where the degree turns into a determinate quantity.
- Space and time concepts are expressed by Aristotle through θέσις (position) and τάξις (order).
- p. 560: the τάξις Aristotle ascribes to time and number turns into a θέσις once time is gathered between fixed bounds (the 'remarkable word Zeitraum') or space is viewed as that which persists. Between the fixed bounds one then seeks fractional magnitudes, with ever denser divisions drawn in thought.

The only quasi-mathematical idea is this last one: an order is made positional by fixing endpoints and interpolating fractions ever more densely. It is a philosophical gloss on constructing a continuous magnitude from a dense order. Nothing is computed. Riemann adds no commentary of his own on this page; his bracketed remark '[R.]' is on the next page.

results.what: Excerpt of Herbart's claim (De attractione elementorum, 1812, §27) that the continuum notion can be 'purged'. Matter's filling of space reduces to 'imaginary notions' that do not apply to the simple reals.
results.modern_name: Herbartian metaphysics of space and matter: intelligible space, the 'Reale', the continuum as a construction of thought

results.what: Leibniz quotations on the vinculum substantiale, composite substance and relations residing only in the mind (Des Bosses correspondence, Dutens II 320-322).
results.modern_name: Leibniz's vinculum substantiale; his doctrine of relations

results.what: Herbart's discussion of Aristotle's categories. Covers ποσόν/ποιόν, intensive (μᾶλλον καὶ ἧττον) versus extensive magnitude, continuous versus discrete magnitude, and τάξις turning into θέσις by interpolating ever denser fractions between fixed bounds.
results.modern_name: Philosophy of magnitude: intensive vs extensive quantity; the dense order as precursor to the continuum
results.usually_credited_to: Aristotle (Categories, Physics); J. F. Herbart (Werke VII)

results.what: Riemann's own engagement with Herbart's metaphysics and philosophy of space as background to his Naturphilosophie and his geometry.
results.usually_credited_to: Documented by E. Scholz (1982) and others

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely excerpts and reading notes from Herbart and Leibniz, plus Herbart's commentary on Aristotle's categories. It contains no mathematics by Riemann. Riemann's study of Herbart, including these Naturphilosophie notes, is well documented (Scholz 1982; Werke, Nachträge).

checkable.asserts: Illustrates the only quasi-mathematical idea on the page: between fixed bounds one can always insert further fractions, so the rationals are densely ordered. This is a trivial illustration, not a claim made on the page.

transcription_corrections: 'als Untermerkmale[?] lang der Eigenschaft' most likely reads 'als Unterarten der Eigenschaft', i.e. ποσόν and ποιόν as sub-kinds of property.

In 'aber auch Formen der Verbindung' context and the reference line, 'Psychologie Bd. 2. §. 144. W. VI. 311' looks right, but the following abbreviations ('Allg. Metaph.') are uncertain in the image; 'W. III 417' and 'W. Bd. I. §. 141' appear correct.
'De vinc. subst.' should be expanded as 'De vinculo substantiali'. The heading reads 'Leibn. op. ed Dut. T. II. pag 320'.
'[-est-] fuerit': the struck word before 'fuerit' is short and only partly legible; 'est' is plausible.
'W. S. 560' at the bottom left is written as 'W. S. 560' (a page in Werke VII), continuing from S. 556 and 558.
